search_result.title: Tachevah artists at Pappy's represent growth of desert music scene
search_result.text:
Bruce Fessier

The Desert Sun

March 20, 2017, 7:40 p.m. ET

The world’s best musical artists are coming to the desert in the next six weeks, starting Sunday with the eight-day Virginia Waring International Piano Competition at the Indian Wells and McCallum theaters, followed by Coachella and Stagecoach.

But first, we get to hear some of the desert's best rock, electronic and hip-hop artists at Tachevah, the music showcase presented by The Desert Sun.

As I said in a KCOD interview Saturday, I’ve never seen so much talent competing for the $3,000 grand prize. Ten bands are performing Thursday at Pappy and Harriet’s in Pioneertown and March 30 at the Palm Canyon Roadhouse in Palm Springs, and I couldn’t possibly pick a favorite to go on to the finals May 18 at The Date Shed in Indio.

KCOD INTERVIEW: Hear Tachevah discussed on air

Only two bands are returning from past Tachevah live showcases. The BrosQuitos finished second at last year’s finals and received $1,000, thanks to the generosity of judge Elizabeth Vargas. Elektric Lucie made it to the finals two years ago.

Labor Day sales are heating up: Shop the best deals before they're gone

That’s one of the remarkable things about this showcase. There’s an amazing new generation of talent every year. We always worry about topping the previous year’s final show. But great new bands pop up every year.

Many of this year’s acts have already done bigger things beyond the desert. They're returning to showcase their skills on our website and to talent scouts at the showcase. Check out who's playing this free show at Pappy’s, being emceed by Teddy Quinn. In order of appearance from 6:30 p.m., they are:

Daytime Moon

Daytime Moon is a psych-rock trio from Joshua Tree that draws on the high desert’s other-worldly nature. Their songs are written “from personal experiences and poems written in altered states of consciousness,” they say on their website, following in the tradition of artists such as Jim Morrison, Gram Parsons and The Eagles.

Singer-guitarist Brent Simpson said he actually came up with the band's name before the lineup coalesced.

“We were outside on a break from writing in Joshua Tree, really trying to brainstorm and we looked up in the sky and saw it," Simpson said. "The Daytime Moon. It fits us well. We are huge believers in alien conspiracies and other-worldly dimensions. Daytime Moon is something much greater than us all combined. It kind of looks like God's finger nail giving us a thumbs-up and telling us ‘You’re doing good!’”

The current trio got together when Simpson’s car overheated in Joshua Tree. Joseph Gonzales, a drummer who had just moved back to town from Las Vegas, happened to be walking down the street. They got together and started jamming and clicked. They needed a bassist, so Gonzales recommended Malachi Rosmino, who he had played with in a high school hard rock band.

“He was really good,” Simpson said, “probably a little too good to be playing with us. But we all had such fluidity. It was almost like ESP.”

Daytime Moon isn’t just a meandering, shoe-gazing psychedelic band. Simpson’s influences include Jimi Hendrix, Bob Dylan, Jimmy Page, Robert Smith, Blink 182, Alkaline Trio and the Beatles. His basset hound is named Sgt. Pepper. And they have the ambition to break out of the desert.

“Malachai has two adorable sons that he has made super proud,” Simpson said. “We all have something burning in us, telling us not to dream our life, but live our dream, and I really feel like we are doing it.”

Arek Religa

Religa, a solo guitarist from Poland, also was turned on to music by the Beatles as a teenager. But he was drawn more by the reaction the musicians were getting.

“it was faces of all the girls and how they reacted to these two guitarists,” he said. “I guess it's nothing new and I'm not the first one.”

Then he started listening to more guitar-showcase music.

“I remember when I heard for the first time “Samba Pa Ti” by Carlos Santana,” he said. “It blew me away, and to this day Carlos is one of my idols along with Ritchie Blackmore, Michael Schenker, Eddie Van Halen, Jimmy Page, Pat Metheny, Mark Knopfler, Al Di Meola and many, many more.”

Religa moved from Poland in 2000 and spent 13 years in Chicago before moving to California. He’s won a slew of awards, including Best New Age Artist at the Hollywood Music Awards for his song, "Island of My Dreams, Part 1.” He was second runner-up in Guitar Player Magazine's “Guitar Superstar 2011” competition. But he loves the desert and is looking for a way to use it as a base of operations for touring and writing new music.

“I'm not sure what inspires me, and I don't think about it too much,” he said. “Inspirations happen and it's OK. To be honest (Tachevah) will be the third time I will be performing in this area and the second time in my life as a solo artist. But hopefully, it's just the beginning.”

Shawn Don

Shawn Don is the stage name for hip-hop artist Shawn Isaac, who grew up in the desert, got an MBA and is now living in Rancho Mirage. He's still active in Las Vegas and L.A. He’s recorded with John Legend, Snoop Dogg, DJ Mustard and Kurupt and played the Venetian/Palazzo in Vegas. But he's also played B.B. Ingle’s New Year's Eve Party at the Hard Rock Hotel Palm Springs and Zelda’s CodyPalooza.

He’d like to tour, but he’s found professional talent in the desert to be able to run his company from here, including producer G-walk, album artist Paul Hasas, and stylist Aide Lopez.

“The desert is fuel to my fire,” he said. “My family, core team, and community are out here. And we have awesome outlets like The Desert Sun that support us musicians. So, those intangibles are more important to me and my music than the tangibles a bigger city might be able to offer.”

Shawn Don submitted a video to the Tachevah Music Showcase, called “Coachella,” that perfectly captures the evolution of the desert from being the playground of Frank Sinatra's Rat Pack to a cool new place influenced by the Coachella festival. It’s an example of the kind of content he’d like to add to the rap genre.

“I want to be different than most artists who perpetuate the ever-present themes of sex, drugs, violence, cussing, and negativity,” he said. “It's such a played-out narrative. There's so much more to life than that.”

Kayves

If Daytime Moon reflects that intangible high desert sound, Kayves, an electro-rock band from Cathedral City, is representative of the new low desert spirit found in the fine art being exhibited by Desert X and artist/curator Cristopher Cichocki.

Their sound conjures images of a wind whistling through the wildflowers. Their name has the same ambiguity as the fine art installations on the desert.

“Our band name, Kayves, does not really have significant meaning,” said guitarist Oscar Rico. “The way we decided our name was based on our sound. Since Danny (Gonzalez) likes using a lot of delay on his guitar and I like using reverb with slight delay, it reminded us of echoes in a cave, and that is how the name Kayves came about, except with a slight spelling twist.”

Gonzalez also plays with Alchemy, a past Tachevah semi-finalist with a similar sound. The band featuring Nick Hernandez on vocals, with Edgar Limon on bass and Adrian Romero on drums, also is influenced by Joy Division, Bloc Party, Interpol, The Cure and Tame Impala. But their sound is distinctively native.

“As young kids in middle school, going to shows at warehouses and venues (in the desert) had a huge impact on us,” said Rico. “I remember talking among each other and saying that we wanted to do that and perform for our friends.

“I think the desert definitely impacts our music and gives it a unique sound. The desert itself gives off an aura of creativity, which is why many artists come to the desert to create their art. I don’t think it is only artists who feel this way, but everyone who comes to the desert and experiences this strange place.”

The BrosQuitos

The BrosQuitos of Desert Hot Springs are perhaps the youngest artists in Tachevah, but, with this third straight trip to the semi-finals, no one has appeared in the live showcases more often. They barely missed winning last year’s competition for a separate prize from judge Spike Edney of Queen for a recording date at the Pink Satellite Studio in Joshua Tree. Then they finished second again to the band brightener in the finals.

So, you may already know the BrosQuitos’ story. Like Daytime Moon and Arek Religa, frontman James Johnston was first inspired by the Beatles. The band’s biggest influence remains Two Door Cinema Club, which is playing in this year’s Coachella.

BROSQUITOS: The back story

They had a recording deal going into last year’s Tachevah with the Inland Empire label, Downpour Records, and their debut album is expected to drop May 12. Johnson says they’ll be playing some new music from that album. They’ll also be playing with $5,000 worth of equipment they earned by winning the Battle of the Bands at the Riverside County Fair and National Date Festival in Indio in February.

Johnson knows the BrosQuitos have to make their money in today’s industry by touring, but he said the desert always will be an inspiration.

“This place is open and welcoming,” he said. “There is plenty of places you can go, and simply enjoy serenity. I think that's very important for songwriting, and it's very hard to do something like that in L.A. Besides that, L.A. will always have an epicenter for entertainment, but the desert is fast approaching that same etiquette.”

The remaining five Tachevah bands will be previewed next week before the March 30 live showcase at the Palm Canyon Roadhouse.

search_result.title: Fans predicted Taylor Swift's '1989' reveal. Do they know what's next?
search_result.text:
Aug. 16, 2023 Updated Aug. 19, 2023, 2:16 p.m. ET

For many fans it was no surprise Taylor Swift announced the release of her “1989 (Taylor’s Version)” album at her final Los Angeles show on Aug. 9.

August is the 8th month of the year and Wednesday was the the 9th day of the month, the last two digits of the album, so how could the news not be coming? Not to mention the last day of the initial U.S. leg of the Eras tour. Also, the “I Can See You” music video from her “Speak Now (Taylor’s Version)" album, which came out last month, featured a subtle street sign that read “1'-9'' - 8.9tv.”

“It was the 20th stop of the tour. And it would have been almost too poetic for it to have been the 19th week,” said Eric Cmar, a 33-year-old Swiftie from LA.

Fans know by now that dates and numbers carry far more meaning in the fandom. Nearly every decision Swift makes can feel like it comes with an extra layer of foreshadowing as she has a history of hiding cryptic clues in her work. And while fans don’t have a 100% accuracy in solving these mysteries, their guesses can’t be overlooked.

Need a news break? Check out the all new PLAY hub with puzzles, games and more!

Once “1989 (Taylor’s Version)” releases on Oct. 27, the record-breaking artist will only have two more albums to re-record so she can own all her work, bringing Swifites to the resolution of their favorite guessing game. This includes her debut 2006 album “Taylor Swift” and her 2017 record “Reputation,” her sixth album and the last made under Big Machine.

“We think ‘debut (Taylor's version)’, and then ‘Reputation (Taylor's Version)' is going to come out in that order,” said Brandy Kaminsky, a 25-year-old Swiftie from Colorado. “In a lot of her new music videos, she'll have curlier hair like when she was in her earlier eras.”

Kaminsky posted a video on TikTok Thursday she made with a friend at work of them sharing their idea for the order of the next albums.

In the video, they point at fan made artwork of the elevator in the “Bejeweled” music video, released on Oct. 24, 2022, where Swift enters an elevator with 13 buttons, each color coded and properly sequenced to represent an album she made, including "Red (Taylor’s Version)" and "Fearless (Taylor’s Version)". The 13th elevator button was purple foreshadowing the release of "Speak Now (Taylor’s Version)” before officially announcing it.

Except the fan made art from Kaminsky’s video includes 17 buttons representing the rerecordings for “1989”, “Taylor Swift”, “Reputation” and her next original album, especially in that order. Kaminsky said the Aug. 9 announcement confirmed that the fan art theory is accurate in predicting the next few albums.

However, Cmar argues “Reputation (Taylor’s Version)” would be the next to drop and also predicts she will complete her recording journey by dropping her debut album on her birthday Dec. 13, 2024.

“Debut last just like an exclamation point on owning her masters. Like I finally own my name. Yeah,” Cmar said. “Dec. 13, 2024, is a Friday new music is released on Fridays so it would be almost all too poetic for her to release her version of her debut album on her birthday.”

Swifites live for being detectives

Kaminsky said she believes Swift always has the next five to ten years of her music planned out so she finds ways to make the promotion of it as exciting as possible.

“Swifties are crazy but most of the time we’re right because we know her. We've known her, we watched her and loved her and sang along with her since 2006,” Kaminsky said. “So those little Easter eggs she drops, there's so many of us that come together and say ideas that most of the time the fandom is right.”

While Cmar understands some fans can get overwhelmed by the amount of effort to analyze clues, he said he’s grateful the singer attached this thrilling adventure to her fan culture.

“It's fun for us. It costs nothing for us but our time and we already enjoy doing it anyway,” Cmar said. “What's cool about any fan interaction with any artist is that you can take whatever you want out of that interaction. Whether it's just their music, or their persona, or their personality, or fun little Easter egg hunts in messages, captions, music videos, tour outfits.”

What is Taylor Swift’s rumored lost 'Karma' album?

Fans have long suspected Swift was supposed to release an album titled “Karma” in 2016 but chose to release “Reputation” in 2017 where she lyrically addressed her public perception following celebrity drama.

Fans noticed Swift changing her appearance by bleaching her hair and chopping it short after releasing "1989” leading theorists to believe she was insinuating a new era. However, when “Reputation” dropped in 2017 the aesthetic of the album and her look did not match. Also, in the music video for the lead single “Look What You Made Me Do,” Swift wore an orange jumpsuit in a cold cage and later sang in the lyric “All I think about is karma.”

“There's this Taylor that's in the video. That's like cutting off the wings of an airplane that was supposed to be an album that she spray paints reputation on,” said Moriah Childress, a 29-year-old Swiftie from Texas. “So, there was this album that was supposed to come out before 'Reputation,' but she had to scrap it and made 'Reputation' instead.”

In the fan art from Kaminsky’s music video, a 17th orange elevator button sits at the top as fans theorize the color orange will be the visual theme for the album. Kaminsky said she always ends her performances on the Eras tour with the song Karma before exiting through an orange door, signifying that concept.

Cmar said one of the most notable indicators of a Karma album is the music video for the song “The Man,” where there’s a scene of a man peeing in front of a wall with the names of multiple albums spray painted on as well as the word “Karma” twice. Swift later released a song titled “Karma” in her 2022 album “Midnights.”

“With the man wall music video moment, that karma being on there twice to me alluded to it's more than just this like single,” Cmar said. “It's on there twice, like it's extra emphasis.”

search_result.title: Jeff Buckley's Memphis home turned into Airbnb: A look at the project
search_result.text:
Sept. 24, 2024, 6:02 a.m. ET

Long a site of pilgrimage for fans from around the world, the modest Midtown cottage that was the last home of singer Jeff Buckley soon will be available for more than social-media photo ops and sidewalk-shot YouTube videos.

“I want this to be in homage to him, but not like a hipster’s Graceland,” said David Lorrison, a real estate agent and longtime concert booker who is working with developer Eric Goode to make the property again available for occupancy.

Purchased for $143,800 in March by Goode Development, the somewhat dilapidated, roughly 900-square-foot house at 93 N. Rembert is being repaired and restored, for use as an Airbnb or for possible sale, with serious Buckley enthusiasts the most likely patrons. The house should be ready by Thanksgiving, developers say.

“Nobody in Memphis was paying attention to the house,” said Lorrison, noting that the 1920 two-bedroom home had been unoccupied for about a year and left to molder, without gas, water or electricity. “But when you look online, you see people are coming here from all over. They drive for miles to make videos of the house and trace Jeff’s steps in Memphis.”

The project comes at a time of renewed media interest in Buckley, in recognition of the 30th anniversary of “Grace,” the only studio album the singer completed and released before his death. Meanwhile, growing numbers of young listeners are discovering and celebrating Buckley's music on TikTok and other digital platforms, attracted by the haunting quality of the singer's ethereal voice and intimate lyrics.

Need a news break? Check out the all new PLAY hub with puzzles, games and more!

'A singular talent'

The son of tragic folk/pop star Tim Buckley, who died of a drug overdose in 1975 at the age of 28, Jeff Buckley drowned in the Wolf River Harbor — essentially, a channel of the Mississippi — on May 29, 1997, after wading into the water to swim near the Mud Island monorail, in an apparently exuberant mood. He was 30.

Buckley’s body was found in the Wolf River on June 4. He apparently had been caught in the wake of a passing tugboat. The Shelby County Medical Examiner ruled the death an accidental drowning.

Inspired by his friendship with the Grifters, a local postpunk band, Buckley, who grew up in the Los Angeles area, had been in Memphis close to a year, working on new material, recording at Easley-McCain studio, and performing regular but unadvertised shows at Barristers, a punk club in a Downtown alleyway.

“Jeff Buckley was beautiful to behold" and "a singular talent,” but “Memphis allowed him a chance to be a pretty regular guy,” wrote music historian and documentary filmmaker Robert Gordon, in a chapter about Buckley in his 2018 book, “Memphis Rent Party.”

According to Gordon, Buckley came to Memphis “to be free” from the “heat” of music-industry pressure. “Jeff Buckley had fame and came here to lose it,” wrote Gordon, who befriended the musician.

Instead, the singer’s fame and popularity have increased almost exponentially since his ultimately tragic Memphis residency.

"Grace,” which stalled at 149 on the Billboard Top 200 album chart during its initial release, has sold some 2.5 million copies since 1997. It was ranked No. 147 on Rolling Stone magazine’s most recent list of the “500 Greatest Albums of All Time.”

Released as a single on the 10th anniversary of Buckley's death, the singer’s cover of Leonard Cohen’s “Hallelujah” reached the top spot on Billboard’s digital charts. In 2013, the Buckley version was inducted into the Library of Congress’ National Recording Registry.

Last week, Forbes reported that Buckley is reaching new heights via that vaunted seismometer of the zeitgeist, TikTok. According to the business magazine, Buckley’s recording “Lover, You Should Have Come Over” is “surging in popularity” and has entered the TikTok top 20 for the first time, "as users on TikTok have been choosing the tune to soundtrack their short-form videos." Also last week, BBC released a new documentary, "Jeff Buckley Forever," narrated by Guy Pearce, with recollections from Patti Smith, Robert Plant and Chrissie Hynde, among others.

Destination home

Both Goode and Lorrison (a Realtor with Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices/Taliesyn Realty) are long-connected with the local music scene. Under the name "Eric 'The Hit Man' Goose," the 56-year-old Goode — who still plays in bands — was half of the alternative-rock deejay team on radio's "The Buzz & Eric Show," found on various stations in the 1990s. Meanwhile, Lorrison, 54 — a sometime chef as well as music promoter — was significant as the founder and original owner of the Hi Tone Cafe, booking such national acts in the club's original location near Overton Park as Iris Dement and Jonathan Richman, along with numerous local bands.

So, the two men are aware that some fans and Memphis acquaintances of the singer might object to the commercialization of the house. But while the profit motive is undeniable, Lorrison says the refurbishing (the Jay Alan Schwartz Electric Co. restored the power) is both a "tribute" to the singer and an acknowledgment of the fact that the home — even in a state of disrepair — was a magnet for Buckley enthusiasts and music tourists.

MEMPHIS MUSIC: Memphis teens in rock band Above Jupiter have big plans for future after dropping debut LP

Also undeniable is the fact that many people are attracted to the homes of the notable departed, especially when the deceased person — whether Elvis or James Dean (lionized in his childhood town of Fairmount, Indiana) or Edgar Allan Poe (whose student room at the University of Virginia has been preserved) — died at a relatively young age.

Situated among several eccentric dwellings on an eclectic block of Rembert, the former Buckley house makes sense as a music-tourist destination. It's not far from the historic Overton Park Shell (the still active music venue where Elvis made his public performing debut in 1954), Ardent Studios (where such artists as ZZ Top, Alex Chilton and the Replacements cut records), and the clubs of Madison Avenue.

Lorrison plans to furnish the interior with period-appropriate furniture, although the only piece now inside the house is a long church pew. That might be incongruous in some circumstances, but it seems appropriate for a singer whose most popular album is "Grace" and whose voice and visage frequently are characterized as "angelic."

Of course, furniture wasn't particularly important to Buckley. “He just kind of camped out in there,” said Memphis music writer Andria Lisle, who hung out with Buckley, along with such other Memphians as Gordon, David Shouse of the Grifters, and David’s wife, Tammy Shouse.

“The house was really spare,” Lisle said. “It was a tiny, wonky, Midtown house, typical for that neighborhood. He borrowed a gorgeous Victorian couch from David and Tammy, but other than that he kind of just had a phone, an answering machine, and a mattress. He always had a pile of books and CDs. He moved from room to room, following the sunlight."

On a recent weekday morning, sunlight bathed the front room, illuminating the newly uncovered pine floors and three framed portraits of Buckley that Lorrison had spaced along the church pew. The single-story home's blue metal roof and freshly painted blue-and-white exterior glowed.

Resting on top of a small hill, the building boasts such a basic, rectangular design, with its center doorway flanked by large windows, that it might be the house in a children's drawing.

Lorrison said he was aware that Buckley had become more than a cult figure in the years since the singer's death; even so, he was not expecting the torrent of Buckley-connected "content" that has appeared in the months since he and Goode began working on the house.

The online enthusiasm for the singer feels like a good omen, he said. "It's been almost serendipitous, in a way," he said. "Every day, it seems like there's another article or another video."

search_result.title: As major powers meet in Asia, the rest of the world is pressed to pick ...
search_result.text:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story appeared in CNN’s Meanwhile in China newsletter, a three-times-a-week update exploring what you need to know about the country’s rise and how it impacts the world. Sign up here.

Hong Kong —

World leaders are converging in Phnom Penh this weekend for the first in a series of international summits in Southeast Asia over the coming week, where divisions between major powers and conflict threaten to overshadow talks.

The first stop is the Cambodian capital where leaders from across the Indo-Pacific will meet alongside a summit of Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) leaders, followed next week by a meeting of the Group of 20 (G20) leaders in Bali and of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Bangkok.

The stacked diplomatic line-up will be a test of international appetite for coordination on issues like climate change, global inflation and rising food prices on the back of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and economic recovery from the Covid-19 pandemic – and the first time that all three events are being held in person since the outbreak began in 2020.

Sharp geopolitical divisions of the type not seen in decades loom over this political calendar, as the war in Ukraine has radically transformed Russia’s relationship with the West, the top two global economies US and China remain locked in intensifying competition, and the rest of the world is pressed to pick a side.

Whether Russian leader Vladimir Putin will make any appearance during the stretch of diplomatic dates remains uncertain. Both US President Joe Biden and Chinese leader Xi Jinping are expected to attend two of the summits in Southeast Asia – a region that has long been ground-zero for influence-jockeying between Beijing and Washington.

Xi is re-emerging on the world stage after years without travel during the pandemic, having secured a norm-breaking third term in power, while Biden heads east fresh from a better-than-expected performance by his party in the US midterm elections. Both would be expected to pitch their country as a stronger partner and more responsible global actor than the other.

The two will meet face-to-face on Monday on the sidelines of the G20, their first in-person encounter since Biden’s election, the White House said on Thursday. Beijing on Friday confirmed Xi’s travel plans to the G20 and APEC summits, and said he would hold bilateral meetings with Biden and several other leaders.

Talks between the two could help to avert an escalation of tensions between the powers. But for the leaders meeting during the string of summits in coming days, cinching robust agreements on tackling global issues – already a tough bargain at the best of times – will be a challenge.

Police officers in Phnom Penh close the roads to traffic around the site of the ASEAN summit, which meets from November 10. Chris Humphrey/picture alliance/Getty Images

Divided world

Even the most regional of the meetings, the ASEAN summit of Southeast Asian leaders – which kicked off in Phnom Penh on Friday and is slated to address strengthening regional stability as well as global challenges – will reflect fractured world politics, experts say.

But unlike the other major meetings, which may be more squarely focused on the fallout from the war in Ukraine, ASEAN leaders are entering the summit and related meetings this weekend under pressure to address a spiraling conflict within their own bloc: as Myanmar remains in turmoil and under military rule nearly two years after a brutal coup ousted the democratically elected government.

Differences between Southeast Asian countries on how to handle that conflict, compounded by their criss-crossing allegiances with great powers – and a reticence from the bloc to appear to take sides between the US and China – will all impact how much the group can agree on and what it can accomplish across the gamut of summits, experts say.

“Normally this season would be very exciting – you have three major world summits in Southeast Asia – Phnom Penh, Bali and Bangkok,” said Thitinan Pongsudhirak, director of the Institute of Security and International Studies at Chulalongkorn University’s Faculty of Political Science in Bangkok.

“But (ASEAN) is very much divided on Russian aggression, on the Myanmar coup crisis, on China’s belligerence in the South China Sea and so on, and this means that ASEAN is in bad shape,” he said.

At a United Nations vote last month, seven of the 10 ASEAN countries, including the Myanmar representative who is not backed by the ruling military, voted to condemn Russia’s annexation of four regions of Ukraine, while Thailand, Laos, and Vietnam abstained.

But ASEAN as a bloc has also taken a step to tighten ties with Kyiv at this week’s events, signing an amity and cooperation treaty with Ukraine in a ceremony with Ukrainian Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba in Phnom Penh on Thursday.

The bloc aims to use consensus among its states as its strength when it brings larger world players to the table, for example in its adjacent East Asia Summit that brings together 18 Indo-Pacific countries, including Russia, China and the United States, and also meets this weekend.

“If ASEAN cannot get its house in order, if ASEAN cannot rein in a rogue member like the Myanmar military regime, then ASEAN loses its relevance,” Pongsudhirak said. “On the other hand, if ASEAN is united, if it can muster commitment and resolve … it can have a lot of pulling power.”

Conflict and competition in Southeast Asia

Nearly two years since the military coup crushed Myanmar’s fledgling democracy, rights groups and observers say freedoms and rights in the country have deteriorated sharply; state executions have returned and the number of documented violent attacks by the ruling military junta on civilian infrastructure, including schools, has surged.

Numerous armed rebel groups have emerged against the ruling military junta, while millions of people have resisted its rule through forms of civil disobedience.

The weekend’s summits in Phnom Penh will pull the conflict back into international focus, as Southeast Asian leaders try to find a path forward, after Myanmar’s ruling junta failed to implement a peace plan negotiated in April of last year. The country remains part of ASEAN, despite calls from rights groups for its ejection, but has been barred from sending political-level representatives to key events.

Protestors setup and guard makeshift barricades to block the road during the demonstration against the military coup in Yangon, Myanmar in March 2021. Stringer/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images

ASEAN foreign ministers held a last-ditch attempt to hash out a strategy late last month, with Cambodian Foreign Minister Prak Sokhonn, who chaired the meeting, stressing in a statement afterwards that the challenges were down to “the complexity and difficulty of Myanmar’s decades-long protracted conflicts, which has been further exacerbated by the current political crisis.”

But observers have low expectations for a tougher line, at least while Cambodia chairs the bloc, and are already looking to next year when Indonesia assumes leadership in 2023.

Addressing the “ongoing crisis” will be a focus for Biden in talks with Southeast Asian leaders as he attends ASEAN summits over the weekend, the White House said on Tuesday. Since the coup, the Biden administration has launched targeted sanctions against the military regime and held meetings with the opposition National Unity Government.

China, on the other hand, has shown support to the ruling military junta and would be unlikely to back tough action, observers say. A months-long inquiry into the situation in Myanmar released by an international team of lawmakers last month accused Russia and China of “supplying both weapons and legitimacy to an otherwise isolated regime.”

That, too, could have an impact on outcomes this weekend, according to political scientist Chong Ja Ian, an associate professor at the National University of Singapore.

“Because of Russian and (Chinese) support for the junta, any efforts toward a solution by ASEAN would require some form of engagement with them, whether this is to get buy-in or even just non-opposition,” Chong said.

The crisis in Myanmar is not the only area where US and China division may loom over the ASEAN summits, even as issues like China’s aggression in the South China Sea – where Beijing asserts territorial claims that conflict with those of several Southeast Asian countries – may be of lesser importance this year.

ASEAN will hold its usual side summits with both the US and China respectively, as well as other countries, and China’s number two leader, the economy-focused Premier Li Keqiang arrived earlier this week as Xi’s representative.

As Southeast Asian leaders seek to shore up their economic stability, they are likely to raise concerns about the impact of US-China competition on the region, its trade and supply chains, for example in the wake of a US export ban on semi-conductors to China, according to Chong.

“ASEAN states are going to try and find some way to navigate all this, and will be looking to both Beijing and Washington to see what sort of leeway they can provide,” he said.

search_result.title: NC Sen. Ted Budd speaks on Helene recovery at G20
search_result.text:
Sept. 2, 2026, 5:03 a.m. ET

Budd said he could oppose a supplemental spending bill without additional disaster aid.

He and Gov. Josh Stein are discussing how much more Congress should provide.

Local governments, Budd said, are finally seeing long-delayed reimbursements begin to move.

ASHEVILLE - U.S. Sen. Ted Budd used a visit to the G20 meetings in Asheville Sept. 1 to press for more federal money for Tropical Storm Helene recovery, defend the Trump administration’s handling of delayed reimbursements and argue that stronger economic growth — rather than a greater emphasis on climate change — would make communities better prepared for future disasters.

The stakes remain enormous nearly two years after the Sept. 27, 2024 storm. North Carolina now estimates Helene caused $60 billion in damage and recovery needs, including $44.4 billion in direct damage. As of June 30, the federal government had approved, allocated or awarded about $9.7 billion for the recovery, according to the Governor’s Recovery Office for Western North Carolina.

Budd vowed in June to vote against any supplemental appropriations package that did not include more money for Helene recovery. The legislation under discussion centered on military spending but also contained aid for Florida farmers who suffered weather-related losses. While Budd admits funding for those particular needs is critical, he has not lost sight of the region's ongoing needs.

“If you're going to add extra things outside supporting our warfighters and our military, let's make sure that you're including Western North Carolina too,” Budd told the Citizen Times at the Omni Grove Park Inn Sept. 1.

Gov. Josh Stein has sought another roughly $10 billion from Washington, revising an earlier request as federal and state money has been awarded and damage estimates have changed. The June request includes more than $3 billion for housing, about $3 billion for local infrastructure and $1 billion for water, wastewater and stormwater projects.

“The governor and I are in discussions on this and how we come to the calculation of what the right number is,” Budd said. “But I can guarantee you that 'zero' is the wrong number.”

Budd has repeatedly criticized the Biden administration over the federal response to Helene. Democratic President Joe Biden was a lame duck president five weeks after the storm, and was out of office just over three months later. President Donald Trump and his "recovery czar" Michael Whatley have now been at the helm for more than 20 months. Budd returned first to the storm’s earliest days, describing saturated ground and extraordinary rainfall before turning to Trump’s visits to the region and his administration’s response.

“Actually, even before day 1, at the end of this storm, early October (2024) he was down in Swannanoa. He was in Black Mountain. He was checking this out. He was on the phone. He's done a fine job, and he's never let up, and that's one of the things that I hear from Western North Carolinians — please don't forget about us,” Budd said. “President Trump never has.”

Much of Budd’s confidence now rests with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, the former Oklahoma senator who took over DHS earlier this year, and FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton, who was confirmed Aug. 10. Budd said Mullin flew to Asheville soon after taking office and accompanied him to Bat Cave. He also pointed to their shared backgrounds outside government.

“He puts great people around him,” Budd said. “He cuts through red tape, and he puts great folks in spots like the FEMA administration and Cam Hamilton.”

Promises vs. performance

That leaves a distinction increasingly important to county managers, town managers and finance officers across the mountains — the difference between federal dollars announced in Washington and reimbursements that reach local accounts.

FEMA project data dated Aug. 28 showed $2.484 billion in federal obligations statewide across 2,942 Helene projects. In nine heavily damaged WNC counties examined by the Citizen Times, $558.1 million had been obligated across 1,201 projects. But an obligation makes federal money available for an approved project and does not establish when a county or municipality actually receives the cash. The state’s latest quarterly report does not separately publish a consolidated total for money deposited with local governments. As of June 30, it listed about $2.35 billion in FEMA Public Assistance funding as allocated or disbursed among state agencies, local governments and nonprofits.

Budd said he has pressed state and county officials to trace delayed reimbursements and identify where money becomes stuck, particularly after local governments spent tens of millions of dollars on debris removal.

“Finally, that money is starting to move and giving some relief to these counties,” Budd said.

Climate change has received less attention at the Asheville G20 meetings than at some previous gatherings. Budd tied disaster resilience instead to the conference’s emphasis on economic growth, energy costs and international stability.

“What we need to focus on, in the theme of this conference, has really been about working together and resilience and growth. So the more we grow, the more we can afford to be resilient, and the more we're resilient, the tougher we are when we do have weather events," Budd said.

Cory Vaillancourt is the Helene Recovery/Investigations Reporter for the Asheville Citizen Times. Find him on X at @The_CoryV or on Signal, via email atcvaillancourt@citizentimes.com or at 912-508-5640.

search_result.title: APEC 2023 in San Francisco includes Biden, Xi Jinping meeting
search_result.text:
Nov. 13, 2023, 5:03 p.m. ET

President Joe Biden is gearing up to welcome Chinese President Xi Jinping and other world leaders in San Francisco on Wednesday at a major economic and trade summit for Pacific powers, according to senior U.S. administration officials.

For weeks, the White House has anticipated Biden and Jinping’s meeting at the APEC summit, which commenced on Saturday. The gathering is expected to draw thousands of protesters in the city during the summit.

The conversation comes at a moment of heavy friction between the two global economies. U.S. officials have said the two leaders hope to establish a framework for healthy, competitive relations going forward.

This week’s summit, which ends Friday, is a fitting setting for the two leaders to work toward this goal after not speaking in-person since the G20 Bali summit last November. The U.S. last held the summit in 2011 in Honolulu and before that in 1993 in Seattle.

Here’s what to know about the APEC, the summit and where the U.S fits into it.

What does APEC stand for?

Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) is an intergovernmental forum of 21 economies throughout the Asia-Pacific region that gather to discuss and promote free trade.

Established in 1989, the forum aims to “create greater prosperity for the people of the region by promoting balanced, inclusive, sustainable, innovative and secure growth and by accelerating regional economic integration.”

APEC's member economies include over 2.9 billion people and make up over 60% of global GDP, according to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade.

Where is the APEC summit in 2023?

San Francisco is hosting the 2023 APEC summit where government and business leaders are convening to discuss economic relations at the Moscone Center.

The city’s board of supervisors president Aaron Peskin said the summit marks the "largest gathering of international players in San Francisco since the United Nations Charter was signed here in 1945," according to CBS News.

What are the different summits during APEC week?

The annual APEC forum hosts various gatherings for government and business leaders including:

Multistakeholder Forum (Nov. 10-13)

Finance Ministers Retreat (Nov. 12)

CEO Summit (Nov. 14-16)

Annual Ministerial Meeting (Nov. 14-17)

APEC Annual Ministerial Meeting Leaders' Plenary (Nov. 16-17)

Business Advisory Council (Nov. 16-17)

Who will attend APEC 2023?

In addition to Biden and Jinping, this year’s APEC summit will gather governmental leaders such as Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, Indonesia's President Joko Widodo and Japanese Prime Minister Fumio Kishida.

The APEC CEO Summit has also drawn tech industry leaders including X (formerly Twitter) owner Elon Musk, Alphabet Inc. CEO Sundar Pichai and Microsoft Corp.'s Satya Nadella.

What is the role of the United States in APEC?

At every APEC forum, the U.S.’s goal has been to pursue a free and fair economic policy agenda that serves American businesses and workers, officials say.

When did the United States join APEC?

The U.S has been a part of the APEC forum since its founding in 1989 when it was an informal ministerial-level dialogue group.

The other 11 founding members include Australia, Brunei Darussalam, Canada, Indonesia, Japan, Korea, Malaysia, New Zealand, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand.

search_result.title: Tourism, trade and workforce take center stage at G20 in Asheville
search_result.text:
Aug. 31, 2026, 5:09 a.m. ET

Vic Isley, of Explore Asheville, projects $1.5M-$2M in direct spending.

John Anglin, business development manager at a road construction firm, says the G20 can spotlight Western North Carolina’s workforce and strengthen the case for continued investment after Helene.

Andrew Nagle, CEO of A-B Emblem in Weaverville, seeks steadier currency and tariff policy.

ASHEVILLE - Asheville’s turn hosting the G20 Finance Track meetings is more than just a few days of hotel bookings, local protests and international attention — for three Western North Carolina business leaders, the gathering is also a chance to showcase a region still rebuilding from Tropical Storm Helene, to attract investment and to put local concerns about tourism, trade, infrastructure and workforce development before some of the world’s most influential economic policymakers.

The world checks in

The immediate benefit begins with bringing visitors to Buncombe County and putting money into local businesses, says Explore Asheville's President and CEO Vic Isley.

Explore Asheville attracts conferences, sporting events and leisure travel to support local jobs and businesses. Isley said the G20 finance track has grown from an estimated 500 attendees to roughly 1,000, making it about the largest event Asheville can accommodate with its available hotel rooms and meeting space. Preliminary estimates based on 500 attendees put direct spending between $1.5 million and $2 million, she said.

But Isley said the larger opportunity may be harder to quantify. The G20 will bring global media attention to a region that, nearly two years after Helene, is still trying to convince visitors that the region is open for business while reminding policymakers that recovery remains unfinished.

Isley said Explore Asheville has booked more conferences and events in Helene’s aftermath than during any comparable period since the organization began in 1983. She sees the G20 as part of an effort to push the visitor economy beyond recovery and into renewed growth, while making the recovery itself part of Asheville’s message.

“This gives us an opportunity as a community and a region to highlight the amazing progress that we've made because of the grit, gumption and determination of the people of Western North Carolina with the local, state and federal resources we have received to date,” Isley told the Citizen Times Aug. 28. “It also enables us to highlight the additional resources and infrastructure that's needed to bring us back even stronger than before.”

Building back, building forward

For John Anglin, business development manager at Branch, the G20 arrives against the physical reality of rebuilding WNC.

Branch is a 100% employee-owned general contractor with more than 1,300 employee-owners. In WNC, Anglin said its work is concentrated heavily in site development and transportation, including emergency rebuilding and permanent repairs after Helene.

Anglin also experienced the disaster from within Yancey County’s response. He served on the county incident management team for eight to nine weeks after the storm and said the scale of destruction made outside assistance indispensable. He cited an early estimate of $4 billion to $6 billion in damage in Yancey County alone, compared with an annual county budget of roughly $37 million to $39 million.

Nearly two years later, Anglin said frustration over the pace of recovery is understandable, but permanent reconstruction requires engineering, permitting and environmental work that cannot be completed as quickly as emergency access was restored. Against that backdrop, he sees the G20’s selection of Asheville as a signal that the region remains worthy of attention from policymakers and investors.

“Man, all of Western North Carolina — we need one another,” Anglin said.

For Anglin, recovery and future growth ultimately converge around workforce. Alongside his work at Branch, he is a Mayland Community College trustee and a member of the High Country Council of Governments Workforce Development Board. He said community colleges, universities and career training programs give the region an asset that should figure prominently in any discussion about investment after Helene.

Anglin pointed to transportation improvements, broadband expansion and the region’s institutions of higher learning as pieces of the economic foundation, but he said the most convincing case for WNC is the way residents responded when the storm tested that foundation.

“If there's one thing that I saw in the aftermath of this storm, it was that no one was complaining about how many hours they were working, how many hours they were volunteering, how much time and effort, blood, sweat and tears they were pouring into helping people,” Anglin said. “I think the testament of our region is the fact that we've got people that are resilient. But more than anything, I think we have the best workforce there is. Period.”

Patches, pesos and policy

The G20 agenda looks different from the factory floor in Weaverville.

A-B Emblem has operated there since 1963, manufacturing embroidered emblems, patches and insignia for customers including scouting organizations, police departments, the U.S. military and NASA.

CEO Andrew Nagle said the family business employs 110 people in Weaverville and also operates factories in Mexico and China, giving it direct exposure to currency swings, tariffs and international banking rules — topics expected to be addressed when global finance ministers meet at the Omni Grove Park Inn Aug. 29-Sept. 1.

Nagle said changes in the Mexican peso can alter labor costs, while tariffs can determine whether customer orders are produced in China, Mexico or the United States. When tariffs on Chinese goods rose sharply, he said, A-B Emblem shifted some production to Mexico rather than passing the full cost increase to customers.

Helene offered the company a different lesson in economic resilience. A-B Emblem’s hilltop factory escaped flooding and structural damage but lost water, power and internet service. Nagle said company managers sat outside a Publix using its Wi-Fi to run payroll. After receiving permission to reopen, an employee repeatedly hauled water from Nagle’s home to keep factory toilets operating.

The plant was down six business days, but Nagle said A-B Emblem paid workers for the missed time anyway. The company later added Starlink service as an internet backup. Nagle said the same principles apply to international business, where companies and countries need alternatives when infrastructure, trade relationships or financial systems fail.

“I think we need to look at that,” he said. “I hope the G20 leaders look at that and go, ‘Yeah, we're kind of in this world together, it's one Earth. It's one world. Let's be good neighbors to each other.’”

Cory Vaillancourt is the Helene Recovery/Investigations Reporter for the Asheville Citizen Times. Find him on X at @The_CoryV or on Signal, via email atcvaillancourt@citizentimes.com or at 912-508-5640.

search_result.title: A guide to Asheville's world-class restaurants ahead of the G20 ...
search_result.text:
Aug. 26, 2026, 5:07 a.m. ET

Local chefs encourage visitors to explore Asheville's broader culinary scene, known for its farm-to-table ethos.

The city boasts numerous restaurants recognized by the Michelin Guide, James Beard Foundation, and Wine Spectator.

Sure it's serious business and tough negotiations when the world's top financial minds gather this weekend for a G20 planning and policy meeting, but surely there's one thing everyone can agree on: We've all got to eat.

G20 organizers have been tight-lipped about the elite group's visit to the Blue Ridge Mountains for the G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors Ministerial conference in Asheville, scheduled from Aug. 29-Sept. 1.

However, The Omni Grove Park Inn & Spa, a historic landmark that opened in 1913 and has a rich history of hosting U.S. presidents, is 100% booked for the dates of the summit. The property's restaurants are unavailable for online booking until Sept. 2.

The Omni Grove Park Inn & Spa's award-winning restaurants can be expected to cater to world leaders. The property features several dining concepts, each with panoramic views of the Blue Ridge Mountains.

But to those world finance greats, we say don't stop there. Asheville has a wealth of restaurants beyond the inn that are worth traveling the globe to visit.

Labor Day sales are heating up: Shop the best deals before they're gone

Chef William Dissen, owner of Appalachian farm-to-table restaurant The Market Place, which has been open downtown for 47 years, said that though dining and traveling plans for the G20 dignitaries are sure to be clandestine, he encourages those visiting to go deeper into the local food culture to enjoy what more the city has to offer.

"Asheville's an internationally renowned tourist destination and mountain town, and our culinary scene has a pedigree that's as great as any other city on the planet," he said. "The access to ingredients, the local farms, the wild ingredients put us on the caliber of any other food city around the world."

While visitors may seek cuisine that reminds them of their home countries, the esteemed chef said the fun of traveling lies in discovering local foodways and fresh heirloom ingredients.

"That's part of the beauty of going to a new destination. You get to learn about the identity and the soul of an area you're in through the food you eat because food tells stories," said Dissen, who has served as a culinary diplomat in the Middle East.

For G20 attendees hungry to break away from the pack to find new experiences and get a true taste of the local food, we've got you covered with a quick study guide to the city's food and beverage scene, beginning with one of the city's treasures, The Omni Grove Park Inn.

Dining at The Omni Grove Park Inn

The Omni Grove Park Inn's Vue 1913, an American brasserie, has famously served U.S. presidents, including Obama and FDR, with their photos displayed at the restaurant, which has earned the Wine Spectator Award of Excellence in consecutive years from 2016 to 2025.

The Presidents Lounge, near the Heritage Ballroom in the Sammons Wing, offers an upscale bar but is a casual place to unwind while fitting in a round of pool.

Edison, Craft Ales and Kitchen (a favorite in times past of Thomas Edison, Harvey Firestone and Henry Ford) is ideal for dining and taking in the cityscape and mountain landscape.

Be sure to stick around for breathtaking evening views at the aptly named Sunset Terrace.

Michelin Award-winning and recommended restaurants in Asheville

Several Asheville restaurants earned Michelin Guide recognition in the inaugural year of the American South's inclusion.

Little Chango (Latin American) and Mother (bakery and cafe) received Bib Gourmand awards, a recognition program that honors restaurants offering the best value for the money. Luminosa (Appalachian-Italian) earned both the Bib Gourmand and Green Star Award for its sustainability practices.

Blind Tiger Asheville, a boutique hotel on East Chestnut Street, was awarded a Michelin Key for the second consecutive year.

Michelin Guide also recommended Addissae Ethiopian Restaurant, All Day Darling, Cúrate Bar de Tapas, Golden Hour at The Radical, Good Hot Fish, Leo's House of Thirst, Soprana at Embassy Suites, Sunny Pointe Café, Table, Tall John's, The Admiral, and Ukiah.

James Beard Award-winning restaurants and chefs

The James Beard Foundation's prestigious national awards program, known as the "Oscars of the food world," has recognized many Western North Carolina restaurants and chefs since 2010, with several rising to the top and earning medals.

This year, Taylor Montgomery, co-founder and executive chef at Montgomery Sky Farm in Leicester, won the regional honor of Best Chef: Southeast. The rustic-meets-chic, fine dining farm-to-table dinners are ticketed, or guests may book a private dining experience.

In 2025, Ashleigh Shanti, chef and owner of Good Hot Fish restaurant, won a James Beard Media Award for her debut cookbook, "Our South: Black Food Through My Lens.”

In 2022, Chai Pani won the Outstanding Restaurant award, and Cúrate, a Spanish tapas bar, won the Outstanding Hospitality award.

World culinary leaders in Asheville

Asheville also is home to chefs who have represented the United States at high-level political events and international platforms.

In 2021, Dissen served as a U.S. culinary diplomat, introducing Southern cuisine and U.S. customs to the people of Doha, Qatar's capital. He also participated in the Arts Envoy Program, a cultural diplomacy initiative, to showcase Appalachian foods and Thanksgiving traditions.

In 2023, Chef Meherwan Irani, cofounder of the Chai Pani Restaurant Group, was invited by Vice President Kamala Harris to prepare the State Department Luncheon in Washington in honor of Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India and his Indian delegation.

In the same year, Chef Katie Button, cofounder of Cúrate, was invited to prepare the meal in honor of Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the Australia State Dinner at the White House, hosted by President Joe Biden and first lady Jill Biden.

Wine Spectator Award-winning cellars

Wine Spectator's 2026 restaurant awards program, recognizing outstanding wine collections, featured 11 Asheville establishments. They're also places that excel for their food and hospitality.

Best of Award of Excellence, two-wine-glass, for the second consecutive year, was granted to:

The Dining Room, a fine dining American restaurant at the historic Biltmore Estate.

Bargello, an Italian and Mediterranean restaurant in the heart of downtown.

Posana's flagship downtown and Biltmore Park/South Asheville modern American restaurants.

The Award of Excellence Award, one-glass rating, was presented to:

Cúrate Bar de Tapas, a James Beard Award-winning and Michelin-recommended Spanish tapas restaurant downtown.

The Blackbird, a Southern Appalachian farm-to-table restaurant downtown.

The Market Place, an Appalachian farm-to-table restaurant operating for 47 years downtown.

Red Stag Grill, in the Grand Bohemian Asheville in the historic Biltmore Village.

The Corner Kitchen, a Southern comfort farm-to-table restaurant in Biltmore VIllage.

Jargon, a modern American restaurant, in West Asheville.

More award-winning restaurants, bar and breweries

Several Asheville establishments have been featured in USA TODAY's annual Restaurants of the Year and Bars of the Year lists since 2024.

The Crow & Quill, Little Jumbo and Potential New Boyfriend were named among the Bars of the Year, ideal for craft cocktails, wine, desserts and entertainment from live jazz to curated vinyl album DJ sets.

Neng Jr.'s (Filipinx), Luminosa (Appalachian/Italian) and Bear's Smokehouse (barbecue) were featured on the Restaurants of the Year lists.

One would be remiss if they missed an opportunity to taste the local craft beverages, including the award-winning craft beer that earned Asheville the name "Beer City."

A few places to begin are at the city's pioneer brewery, Highland Brewing, established in 1994, and the 2026 World Beer Cup-winning breweries: Diatribe, Wicked Weed and Hi-Wire.

There is no shortage of outstanding destinations to get a taste of local mountain traditions and modern innovation or a plate that reminds one of home, far away.

"I hope they come here and see how hard we've all worked to revitalize our city after Hurricane Helene, and they go home and tell everyone about it, and it helps shed a light on some of the recovery still needed here financially," Dissen said. "And to let people know how beautiful our community is, and to come visit for themselves."
